$comment: The tag vocabulary and the shelf families, in ONE place. Before this file existed the family table lived only inside prototype/template.html, which meant no tool could check it and the game was the only thing that knew which tags were real. 1,075 elements — one in seven — fell through that table into a catch-all called Other, and nothing counted them. A vocabulary that only the renderer knows is not a vocabulary; it is a habit.
$rules: families is ORDERED and first match wins. An element matching two families is filed under the earlier one, and tools/categories.mjs reports every such element, because an ambiguous filing is a tagging question that has not been answered.
Every tag on every element must appear in exactly one family's tags list. A tag that appears nowhere is an error, not a new category.
deprecated maps a tag that should no longer be authored onto the one that replaces it. These are not aliases the renderer resolves — they are work to be done, and the checker counts them down.
The folklore shelf overrides all of this: a folklore element is filed under myth whatever it is tagged.

families.name: Folklore
families.note: Everything on the folklore shelf, plus anything tagged as a story. Marked by an absence of source, never by a colour.

families.name: Medicine
families.note: Second in the order, and deliberately. Everything used to be filed by where it came from, so paracetamol sat under Earth & Stone, aspirin and morphine under Growing Things, penicillin and insulin under the microbes. A medicine could only be found by someone who already knew its origin, which is the opposite of what a drawer is for. You look for aspirin under medicine, not under willow.

families.name: Molecules & Cells
families.note: Below the world of things. Past 10⁻⁸ m the drawing language changes to skeletal convention, and this is the drawer that change belongs to.

families.name: Microbes & Fungi
families.note: Organisms too small to see, and the fungi that are not. Fermentation lives here because the agent is the organism.

families.name: Music
families.note: The Hornbostel-Sachs classes are kept as tags because how an instrument makes its sound is the real distinction between them — a piano is a chordophone you strike, and that is a fact about physics, not about repertoire.

families.name: Wild Animals
families.note: Animals nobody keeps. Extinct ones are wild by definition — there is no husbanded mammoth.

families.name: Animals & Dairy
families.note: Kept animals and what comes off them.

families.name: Growing Things
families.note: Plants wild and sown, and the grains that are the oldest crops there are.

families.name: Earth & Sky
families.note: Rock, soil, ocean, air and everything above the air. It was Earth & Stone while it held the sun and the sea.

families.name: Metals
families.note: Its own drawer because metallurgy is its own chain — ore, smelt, alloy, work.

families.name: Building
families.note: Materials and structures that hold something up, and the civic buildings that are what a settlement is for.

families.name: Tools & Made Things
families.note: The largest drawer, and honestly named: anything a person made that is not a building, a meal, an instrument or a medicine. It was called Fire & Tools while it held furniture, plumbing and clothing — a label that had stopped describing its contents.

families.name: Kitchen
families.note: Ingredients, dishes, drinks and the methods that keep them.

families.name: People & Past
families.note: Named people, periods, events, and the hominins that came before us.

families.name: Belief
families.note: What people have held to be true. Distinct from myth: a belief is real as a belief.

families.name: Trade & Society
families.note: Exchange, money, and the institutions built on them.

families.name: Ideas
families.note: Abstractions. hazard lands here only when it is the only tag — carcinogen, mutagen, teratogen, which are concepts. Nicotine carries it as a second tag and matches Growing Things long before this.

families.name: Other
families.note: The catch-all, LAST and named honestly. It used to be chosen by array index, so every unclassified element was not merely uncategorised but actively mis-filed under a heading that looked plausible. A visible Other makes the next tagging gap something you can count.

$deprecatedNote: Each of these is a near-twin of a tag that already existed, authored because nothing stopped it. They still shelve correctly — both members of each pair sit in the same family — so nothing is broken today. They are listed because a vocabulary with two words for one thing gets a third, and because the first tool to disagree about which one is canonical will file the same element two ways.
